Check visible duplication/variant drift/incentives/documented manipulation. Detail, stars, badges or AI detectors cannot certify truth/fakery; incentives are not automatic falsity. Separate usefulness/credibility.

Keep three questions apart: whether a seller's review display can be audited, whether each review reflects a real buyer, and whether the product works; an answer to one settles neither of the others. Record each review's provenance (seller-curated, embedded testimonial, independent platform, imported or syndicated, email- or order-verified, incentivized, unknown) and compare displayed totals with the texts actually read; a failed "load more" or an empty review feed is an access boundary, not evidence of fabrication. Before reading a cross-platform mismatch as manipulation, check imports, order-ID eligibility, earlier product IDs and migrated testimonials. Never judge a product from its seller's own pages: also search independent communities, such as Reddit and specialist forums, where detailed firsthand reports can confirm or contradict the seller's display. Judge whether each decisive review reads as machine-written or is dated before the product went on sale, and give the signs, such as generic praise, no concrete personal detail, a template structure or copied product claims; that judgment is a clue about the display, not proof that a person or an experience is fake. Weigh specific firsthand reports (symptom or function, duration, co-exposures, stop and restart, objective measures) above content-free praise, in both directions: they can raise the probability that some buyers benefit, never establish how many or how much. A questionable review practice and a working product are compatible.

<case id="ReviewProvenanceVersusEfficacy">
A supplement seller's widget claims 600 reviews but shows five old five-star testimonials and returns nothing for the rest; a buyer app shows 490 ratings with generic praise, a few detailed improvements and some nonresponse, and excludes imports without order IDs: explain the incomplete corpus and the different verification rules, allege no fraud from the mismatch or the empty feed, keep both detailed positive and negative buyer reports as low-certainty signals, and give no buyer benefit percentage or efficacy conclusion.
</case>
<case id="SellerPageVersusIndependentForum">
A supplement's site shows static five-star testimonials dated before it went on sale, one of which reads as machine-written; on Reddit, several detailed firsthand reports describe benefit, and some describe none: report the seller's testimonials as unreliable with the signs, keep the Reddit reports as the stronger real-world signal with their limits, and conclude neither that the product is a scam nor that it works.
</case>
